case_analysis.focal_point: Whether time continues to run on a federal term of supervised release while the supervisee is absconding (a fugitive from supervision), such that she is entitled to credit for that period and the court may lose authority to revoke after the original term’s calendar end-date.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(i) concerning delayed revocation; and the statutory scheme governing commencement/expiration of supervised release), with related background principles about jurisdictional time limits raised by the parties (e.g., Bowles v. Russell).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues she is entitled to credit for the time that elapsed on the calendar during which she was not reporting because Congress did not authorize “fugitive tolling” of supervised release; supervised release is a term that runs with time unless the statute expressly provides otherwise, and § 3583(i) supplies the exclusive, limited mechanism for post-expiration revocation (requiring a warrant/summons issued before expiration). Allowing judge-made tolling improperly extends punishment beyond the sentence imposed and the statute’s text, and it risks harsh outcomes given real-world barriers to reentry and compliance highlighted by amici (housing, instability, fear, misunderstanding of obligations).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues absconding should not allow a person to ‘run out the clock’ on supervised release and thereby evade revocation consequences; supervised release is designed to supervise and rehabilitate in the community, and a person cannot receive credit for a period when supervision was impossible because she was a fugitive. The government contends courts may treat absconding as tolling (or otherwise as not counting toward service of the term), and that § 3583(i) should not be read to create a loophole rewarding flight and undermining the supervision system.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (9th Cir. precedent referenced in the district court transcript concerning fugitive tolling and binding circuit law)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that supervised release is functional monitoring, so an absconder has not truly been “supervised” and should not be able to profit by flight. But under a minimalist, text-centered approach, the critical question is what Congress authorized: § 3624(e) contains an express “does not run” stop-clock rule for imprisonment, and § 3583(i) supplies a specific, conditional post-expiration mechanism keyed to a pre-expiration warrant or summons—leaving little room for an extra-statutory fugitive-tolling doctrine without effectively nullifying that condition. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Mont confirms tolling in this area turns on enacted text (there, Congress wrote the stop-clock rule), and Bowles—invoked by Justice Thomas—underscores the institutional costs of courts crafting equitable extensions around congressionally drawn temporal limits on judicial authority. The policy concern about “running out the clock” is real, but Congress addressed it through the warrant/summons trigger; expanding beyond that would extend punishment beyond the term Congress fixed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest contention—that an absconder has not “served” supervised release in any meaningful sense—cannot supply a tolling rule Congress did not enact; the statutory text already specifies when supervised release “does not run” (§ 3624(e)) and separately limits post-expiration revocation to cases with a pre-expiration warrant or summons (§ 3583(i)). Justice Jackson’s reframing that fugitive status prevents “expiration” merely redescribes the same atextual extension of the term, because nothing in §§ 3583 or 3624(e) makes absconding a stop-clock event. As the Chief Justice notes, recognizing fugitive tolling would functionally evade § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons condition and expand punishment beyond the temporal limits Congress authorized. Bowles reinforces the separation-of-powers problem with judicially created temporal exceptions where Congress has drawn specific lines, so any policy fix for “running out the clock” must come from Congress, not this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s structural/textual point—Congress expressly tolls supervised release for imprisonment in § 3624(e) and separately cabins post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) to cases with a pre-expiration warrant or summons—is the best argument against implied fugitive tolling, and I take seriously the Bowles-like concern about courts extending temporal limits on authority. But I do not read our position as an equitable “exception” to § 3583(i); rather, as Justice Jackson suggests, the antecedent question is whether the supervised-release term has actually “run” at all when the defendant makes supervision impossible through deliberate flight. Section 3583’s premise is supervision—monitoring and assistance in the community—and it is at least as natural to say that a defendant who absconds has not “served” that term, meaning § 3583(i)’s post-expiration mechanism never becomes the operative constraint until the term truly expires. Mont’s emphasis that supervised release is about supervision, not just the passage of time, supports treating absconding as preventing the term from running, avoiding a practical loophole that would let defendants defeat Congress’s design by “running out the clock.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Jackson press the strongest functional point: supervision cannot occur while a person absconds, so crediting that time feels like rewarding obstruction. But the statutory scheme already channels that concern through specific textual tools—§ 3624(e)’s express stop-clock rule and § 3583(i)’s limited post-expiration revocation authority keyed to a pre-expiration warrant or summons—so treating fugitive time as preventing “expiration” effectively nullifies Congress’s chosen trigger and invites open-ended extensions beyond the sentence’s temporal limits. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, that move is not just policy-driven; it reconfigures a detailed statutory design in a way Bowles cautions against when courts create extra-textual extensions to congressionally set time limits on judicial power. Given the real-world risk that vulnerable supervisees (housing instability, mental illness) can be deemed “absconders” without strategic flight, I would not adopt a judge-made tolling doctrine absent clear congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is functional: supervision can’t occur while someone is absconding, so it feels wrong to credit that time. But under my pragmatic textualism, that intuition can’t override the statutory architecture Congress actually wrote—§ 3624(e) contains an express “does not run” stop-clock rule for imprisonment, and § 3583(i) separately supplies a carefully administrable post-expiration revocation mechanism keyed to a pre-expiration warrant or summons; adding a free-floating fugitive-tolling doctrine would dilute § 3583(i)’s trigger and effectively extend punishment beyond the sentence without clear authorization, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. Mont matters here not because it invites more tolling, but because it shows this Court grounds tolling in enacted text (there, the explicit stop-clock), which cuts against judicial supplementation. Bowles, while not making § 3583(i) jurisdictional in every respect, reinforces the separation-of-powers concern with courts crafting equitable extensions around congressionally specified temporal limits in a detailed scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Jackson press the most serious point: supervision is a functional regime of monitoring, so an absconder has not meaningfully been “supervised,” and they say that means the term hasn’t truly “expired.” But that argument asks us to replace the statute’s time-based “term of supervised release” with a judicially crafted “availability-for-supervision” condition; Congress, by contrast, wrote a specific stop-clock rule in § 3624(e) and a separate, carefully conditioned post-expiration revocation power in § 3583(i) keyed to a pre-expiration warrant or summons. Reading “expiration” to be suspended by flight would effectively nullify § 3583(i)’s warrant requirement and extend punitive exposure beyond the temporal limits Congress authorized—precisely the separation-of-powers concern Bowles highlights when courts fashion equitable extensions around precise statutory limits. If there is a policy gap, the text shows Congress knew how to write tolling and chose not to do so here, so I would not supply it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Jackson make the best functional point: an absconder has not meaningfully undergone “supervision,” so crediting that time seems to reward obstruction. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Congress built a detailed scheme that (i) expressly tolls supervised release in § 3624(e) for imprisonment and (ii) separately authorizes limited post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) only when a warrant or summons issues before the term’s end; implying a fugitive stop-clock rule would effectively erase that statutory condition and extend supervision beyond the sentence Congress authorized. Mont underscores that tolling in this domain is text-anchored rather than equitable, and Bowles heightens the separation-of-powers concern with judicially crafting exceptions to congressionally drawn temporal limits. The policy worry about “running out the clock” is real, but Congress chose a warrant/summons mechanism to address it, and I do not think we should add an extra-statutory tolling doctrine on top of that choice.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional point—that supervision cannot occur while the defendant absconds—has real intuitive force, and Justice Jackson is right that § 3583(i) presupposes a term that has “expired.” But under a textualist reading, neither intuition nor background equitable principles can supply a tolling rule Congress omitted when it expressly provided one in § 3624(e) and then separately conditioned post-expiration revocation authority in § 3583(i) on a pre-expiration warrant or summons, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. Recasting fugitive time as preventing “expiration” effectively rewrites the statutory computation and dilutes § 3583(i)’s procedural trigger, creating the same kind of atextual extension Bowles warns against when Congress has specified the relevant temporal limits. The policy concern about “running out the clock” is substantial, but the statute’s own solution is prompt issuance of a warrant within the term, not judicial invention of an additional stop-clock rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s expressio unius argument has real force—Congress expressly stopped the clock in § 3624(e) and specified a limited post-expiration mechanism in § 3583(i), so courts must be cautious about adding tolling doctrines. But I am not persuaded this is an “equitable extension” in the Bowles sense; as Justice Alito notes, the antecedent question is whether the supervised-release term can be said to have “run” when the supervisee has made supervision impossible, given that Congress designed the term as active monitoring and assistance rather than mere passage of calendar time. Reading absconding as preventing service of supervision does not nullify § 3583(i); it still governs cases where the term truly has expired (including where the Government delays), whereas fugitive status goes to whether expiration has occurred at all. The statutory scheme should not be construed to reward obstruction by allowing a defendant to defeat Congress’s rehabilitative and public-safety objectives simply by absconding until the stated end date.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3583 establishes a comprehensive scheme for when supervised release runs and when revocation may occur after the term’s expiration, and Congress provided a specific, limited post-expiration mechanism in § 3583(i) that turns on a warrant or summons issued before the term ends. Reading a judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine into the statute would add an exception Congress did not enact—especially given that Congress expressly provided a tolling rule in § 3624(e) for imprisonment—counseling against judicially creating further tolling categories. Our approach in Mont v. United States, construing § 3624(e), underscores that when Congress specifies when supervised release “does not run,” courts should not infer additional stop-clock rules; the proper course is to apply the statutory text and leave policy concerns to Congress. A narrow holding that time continues to run absent a pre-expiration warrant or summons under § 3583(i) respects precedent, avoids expanding punishment beyond the statutory authorization, and promotes institutional legitimacy by adhering to the line Congress drew.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of § 3583 provide the operative rules for when supervised release runs and when a court may act after expiration, and they do not authorize judge-made “fugitive tolling.” Congress expressly provided a limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i), conditioned on a warrant or summons issued before expiration; reading an extra, atextual tolling doctrine into the statute would circumvent that limit and extend punishment beyond what Congress specified. While the Government invokes equitable principles to prevent a supervisee from “running out the clock,” this Court has rejected judicial alteration of statutory time limits and related jurisdictional constraints absent clear textual authorization, see Bowles v. Russell. Historical parole cases like Anderson v. Corall arose under a materially different statutory regime and cannot supply authority to rewrite the supervised-release scheme Congress enacted in § 3583 and related provisions (including the express tolling rule in § 3624(e) for imprisonment).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Supervised release is not merely the passage of calendar time; it is a period of "postconfinement monitoring" and assistance that presupposes the defendant’s availability for supervision, and an absconder cannot plausibly claim to have “served” supervision while deliberately making supervision impossible. Although 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) expressly tolls supervised release during imprisonment "in connection with a conviction," Mont v. United States recognizes the broader structural point that supervised release time does not run when the supervisee is not in a position to be supervised, and credit should not be awarded for such periods. Reading 18 U.S.C. § 3583(i) as the exclusive mechanism would create a perverse loophole allowing defendants to “run out the clock” by flight, undermining the statute’s rehabilitative and public-safety purposes and producing impractical consequences for law enforcement. Bowles v. Russell’s jurisdictional-time-limit concern does not compel the petitioner’s reading here because the question is how to compute the supervised-release term in the first place, not whether a court may disregard an unambiguous statutory deadline.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The supervised-release statute already contains an express tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (for imprisonment), and an express, limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(i) (requiring a warrant or summons issued before the term expires). That structure strongly suggests Congress did not authorize additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling,” and adopting it risks extending punishment beyond the sentence as set and beyond the statute’s text—an outcome this Court has cautioned against when time limits are treated as jurisdictional or strictly constrained by statute, see Bowles v. Russell. While absconding is serious and can be sanctioned, § 3583(i) supplies the remedial path Congress chose, and courts should not create an extra-statutory doctrine that can disproportionately burden vulnerable supervisees facing instability and barriers to compliance. The better reading preserves clear, administrable limits on revocation authority and leaves any broader tolling rule to Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme is governed by 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) and § 3583, and Congress included one explicit tolling rule in § 3624(e) (for “imprisoned in connection with a conviction”) while providing a specific, limited post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) requiring a warrant or summons issued before the term’s expiration. Reading a judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine into this framework risks overriding Congress’s calibrated choices and effectively extending punishment beyond the sentence’s temporal limits, contrary to the usual inference that when Congress specifies exceptions courts should not add others. Mont v. United States underscores that tolling in this area turns on statutory text—there, the Court enforced the textually grounded tolling rule in § 3624(e), not a freewheeling equitable doctrine—supporting the conclusion that absconding is not an additional, unstated tolling trigger. Workability concerns about fugitives “running out the clock” are addressed by § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons requirement and prompt enforcement, rather than by expanding tolling beyond the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text supplies a tolling rule for supervised release in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), but it does not authorize tolling for absconding; under ordinary textual inferences, courts may not create additional exceptions when Congress has specified the ones it wants. Section 3583(i) further confirms Congress’s design by providing a limited, warrant-or-summons-based mechanism for delayed revocation after the term’s expiration—limits that would be undermined by a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine that effectively extends the sentence’s duration. Bowles v. Russell reinforces that courts must respect statutory time limits and may not fashion equitable extensions of congressionally prescribed deadlines. Whatever the policy appeal of preventing a supervisee from “running out the clock,” that argument is for Congress, not the judiciary, given separation-of-powers constraints and the statute’s plain meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3624(e) expressly tolls supervised release during imprisonment, and the absence of any comparable tolling rule for fugitive status strongly indicates Congress did not authorize judge-made “fugitive tolling” (expressio unius), especially given the detailed supervised-release scheme in § 3583. Congress instead provided a specific, workmanlike mechanism for delayed revocation in § 3583(i), which preserves authority only when a warrant or summons issues before the term’s expiration; reading an additional equitable tolling doctrine into the statute risks extending punishment beyond the sentence Congress authorized and blurring jurisdictional limits. Bowles v. Russell underscores that courts should not craft extra-statutory exceptions to congressionally prescribed time limits that constrain adjudicatory authority. Practical concerns about preventing supervisees from “running out the clock” are addressed by § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons requirement and by enforcement tools during the term, not by judicially adding tolling that Congress omitted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of § 3583 indicate that Congress specified when supervised release pauses and when revocation may occur after the term’s expiration, leaving little room for judge-made “fugitive tolling.” Section 3583(i) expressly conditions “[t]he power of the court to revoke” after expiration on a warrant or summons issued before the term ends, and treating absconding as tolling would effectively create an atextual, equitable extension of that power beyond the limits Congress set—an approach Bowles v. Russell cautions courts not to adopt for jurisdictional time limits. Congress also demonstrated in § 3624(e) that it knows how to write tolling rules expressly; its choice in § 3583(i) to extend jurisdiction (not time) suggests the term itself continues to run absent a statutory pause. While the Government’s policy concern about “running out the clock” is serious, the remedy lies with Congress rather than a judicially crafted tolling doctrine inconsistent with the enacted text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583’s structure aims to ensure a meaningful, workable period of community supervision, and it would undermine that scheme to award credit for time when supervision was impossible because the supervisee absconded. Section 3583(i) is best read as a limited delayed-revocation provision (requiring a pre-expiration warrant or summons when the term has otherwise run), not as an affirmative command that the supervised-release clock must run even while the person is a fugitive; Congress’s silence can permissibly leave room for background principles preventing a person from benefiting from flight. While Bowles v. Russell cautions against judge-made equitable exceptions to jurisdictional deadlines, § 3583(i) is triggered only when the term “expires,” and treating fugitive time as not counting toward service prevents the “expiration” premise from arising in the first place. Given the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns, allowing “run out the clock” incentives would weaken supervision and frustrate rehabilitation and public-safety goals embedded in § 3583.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether time continues to run on a federal term of supervised release while the supervisee is absconding (i.e., a fugitive), so that she earns credit toward completion of supervision during that period.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(i) concerning delayed revocation and related timing/jurisdiction questions); more broadly, the statutory framework governing supervised release terms and revocation.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues she is entitled to credit for the period she was absent from supervision, meaning her supervised-release clock kept running even while she was absconding. In her view, supervised release is a statutory term that expires by operation of law after the set length unless Congress expressly authorizes tolling, and courts should not create a judge-made 'fugitive tolling' doctrine that effectively extends supervision beyond the sentence imposed. She also invokes limits on jurisdiction/time extensions and contends the government must proceed within the statutory mechanisms (including those in § 3583(i)) rather than rely on equitable tolling concepts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues petitioner should not receive credit for time spent as a fugitive because absconding prevents supervision from being carried out and would let a defendant avoid consequences for violations by running out the clock. The government defends fugitive tolling (or an equivalent reading of the statutory scheme) to preserve the court’s ability to enforce supervised-release conditions and revoke supervision based on violations discovered or pursued after the supervisee is located, and it characterizes petitioner’s position as creating perverse incentives and undermining the purposes of supervised release.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (Ninth Circuit precedent referenced in the record on fugitive tolling)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s argument that absconding defeats “supervision” has real intuitive pull, but under our statutory sentencing regime that intuition cannot supply a stop-the-clock rule Congress did not write. As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 3624(e) contains the only express “does not run” instruction, and Mont reinforces that tolling must rest on that kind of textual hook rather than a free-floating unavailability principle; fugitivity has none. Section 3583(i) further suggests Congress chose a targeted way to preserve revocation authority post-expiration (timely warrant or summons), and a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would functionally enlarge the sentence beyond the term imposed. Policy concerns about rewarding flight are serious, but, consistent with Bowles and institutional legitimacy, they are for Congress or for enforcement through § 3583(i) and separate prosecution, not judicial invention.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best argument—that an absconder is not actually being “supervised” and thus is not “serving” supervised release—has intuitive appeal, but it asks us to infer a fugitive-tolling rule from a premise Congress did not write into § 3624(e). As the Chief Justice notes, § 3624(e) contains the sole express “does not run” provision (imprisonment), and the negative implication recognized in United States v. Johnson counsels against adding another stop-the-clock category by judicial construction. Mont does not supply a general unavailability principle; it simply applied the specific tolling text Congress enacted, and reading Barrett’s rule into the statute would undermine § 3583(i)’s targeted warrant/summons mechanism by effectively extending supervision beyond the term imposed. Bowles further confirms that when Congress sets temporal limits in a statutory scheme, courts lack equitable authority to extend them based on perceived purpose or anomalies.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s argument that an absconder is not really being “supervised” and therefore is not “serving” supervised release is the most forceful response, and her effort to analogize to Mont highlights the practical anomaly of crediting flight. But under the statutory structure Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Congress expressly specified when supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e) and separately provided a limited, notice-linked post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i); it is not our role to add a second tolling category for fugitivity that effectively extends the sentence. Mont does not supply that missing textual hook because it relied on § 3624(e)’s explicit stop-the-clock language tied to imprisonment, whereas fugitivity is nowhere addressed in comparable terms. Whatever the policy appeal, Bowles reinforces that courts lack equitable authority to enlarge congressionally prescribed temporal limits in a wholly statutory sentencing regime.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that an absconder is not truly being “supervised,” so it is anomalous to credit that time—captures an important real-world intuition, but it still asks us to create a stop-the-clock rule the statute does not supply. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress expressly specified when supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e) and separately crafted a narrow, notice-linked mechanism for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i); that structure strongly counsels against a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine that effectively extends punishment without clear authorization. Mont does not move me toward respondent because, as Justice Thomas notes, it rested on § 3624(e)’s explicit “does not run” language tied to imprisonment—text we do not have for fugitivity—so it cannot justify importing a broader unavailability principle. The government’s incentive concerns are serious, especially for community safety, but they can be addressed through timely warrants under § 3583(i) and prosecution for new crimes rather than judicially enlarging a sentence component in a way that risks undermining notice and fairness.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point is that an absconder is not being “supervised,” so it feels textually awkward to say he is still “serving” a term of supervised release. But that intuition cannot override the statute’s specific stop-the-clock instruction in § 3624(e): as the Chief Justice emphasizes, Mont treated tolling as a matter of the “does not run” language Congress actually enacted, and there is no comparable fugitivity clause to supply that same textual hook. Reading a freestanding “unavailability” principle into the word “term” would effectively create a new tolling category and, as Justice Thomas notes via Johnson’s negative-implication logic, would undercut Congress’s choice to address post-expiration revocation through the concrete, notice-linked warrant/summons mechanism in § 3583(i). On my pragmatic textualism, § 3583(i) is the workable middle ground Congress provided, and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule risks extending the sentence beyond the coherent statutory scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s argument that a fugitive is not truly being “supervised” presses the best textual intuition for respondent, and her Mont analogy highlights the anomaly of crediting deliberate unavailability while tolling involuntary custody. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Mont rested on § 3624(e)’s express “does not run” command tied to imprisonment, and that kind of clear stop-the-clock language is absent for absconding—so a textualist cannot supply it by inference from statutory purpose. Reading a fugitive-tolling rule into the scheme would also erode § 3583(i)’s carefully delimited warrant/summons mechanism for post-expiration revocation, effectively extending a statutory sentence component without congressional authorization, which Bowles’s caution against equitable time extensions reinforces. The policy concern about rewarding flight is real, but under our separation-of-powers role it is for Congress to address by writing additional tolling rules, not for courts to invent them.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point—that an absconder is not meaningfully being “supervised,” so it seems anomalous to credit that time—has real intuitive and purposive force, and I appreciate her effort to analogize to Mont. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Mont’s holding depended on § 3624(e)’s express “does not run” language tied to imprisonment; there is no comparable textual hook for fugitivity, and importing one would be a judge-made enlargement of a statutory sentence component. Section 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism reads to me like Congress’s chosen way to preserve revocation authority when the term would otherwise expire, and recognizing fugitive tolling would substantially dilute that calibrated scheme. Under an institutionalist, precedent- and text-centered approach, the policy concern about incentives to flee cannot justify adding a tolling rule Congress did not enact.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s negative-implication argument from § 3624(e) and his reliance on § 3583(i) are the most serious textual objections, and Justice Thomas’s Bowles-based warning against equitable extensions highlights the legitimacy concern. But I do not read fugitive tolling as an equitable add-on; rather, the question is what it means for a “term of supervised release” to “run” when the defendant has made supervision impossible—an absconder is not “serv[ing]” supervised release in any ordinary, original public-meaning sense, so crediting that period treats deliberate noncompliance as satisfaction of a sentence component. Mont, though grounded in § 3624(e)’s imprisonment clause, supports the broader textual premise that the supervised-release clock is tied to the defendant’s availability for supervision, and it would be anomalous to deny credit for involuntary unavailability (custody) yet award credit for intentional unavailability (flight). Section 3583(i) is best understood as a jurisdiction-preserving backstop when the court acts with a timely warrant/summons, not as an affirmative instruction that time spent as a fugitive must count toward completion, and thus it does not foreclose the more natural reading of “run” in § 3624(e).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that an absconder is not actually being “supervised,” so crediting that time seems anomalous—has real intuitive and policy force, but it still does not supply statutory authority to stop the clock. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Mont rested on § 3624(e)’s express command that supervised release “does not run” during specified imprisonment, and that textual hook is missing for fugitivity; importing a broader “unavailability” principle would effectively add a new tolling category Congress did not enact. Section 3583(i) also matters for procedural fairness: it gives the government a clear, notice-linked tool (timely warrant/summons) to preserve revocation authority, and judge-made tolling would extend the endpoint of a sentence without the same statutory clarity. Under my pragmatic, fairness-focused methodology, the incentive concerns Barrett raises are better addressed through the mechanisms Congress provided (warrants, new charges) than by expanding supervision duration through implication.

John Roberts.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes supply an express tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (time does not run during certain imprisonments), but they do not provide for tolling when a supervisee absconds; under the negative-implication principle applied in United States v. Johnson and reinforced by the Court’s textual approach in Mont v. United States, courts should not create additional, judge-made exceptions. Section 3583(i) further indicates Congress addressed timing and jurisdiction for delayed revocation through a specific mechanism (issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration), undermining the need for an atextual “fugitive tolling” doctrine. A narrow holding that the clock continues to run absent statutory tolling respects the sentence Congress authorized, avoids expanding judicial power beyond the statute, and preserves institutional legitimacy by leaving any additional tolling rule to Congress. Concerns about perverse incentives are better handled through § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons process and prosecution for failure to appear or escape-related offenses, rather than by extending supervision through equitable doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme is statutory, and courts may not add equitable exceptions Congress did not enact. Section 3624(e) contains the lone express tolling rule (for imprisonment of 30 days or more), and under the textual inference recognized in United States v. Johnson, 529 U.S. 53 (2000), the inclusion of that exception counsels against a judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine. Section 3583(i) further confirms Congress specified the limited circumstance in which revocation may occur after expiration (upon a timely warrant or summons), which would be undermined if courts could extend supervision by implied tolling. Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), reinforces that courts must respect congressionally prescribed limits rather than enlarge them through judicial doctrines.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes contain an express tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (for imprisonment of 30+ days), but Congress did not include comparable language tolling a term when a defendant absconds, and we should not create a judge-made extension of a sentence where Congress chose not to authorize it. Section 3583(i) confirms Congress knew how to address timing and delayed revocation by extending jurisdiction only when a warrant or summons issues before expiration, which undercuts any implied, open-ended “fugitive tolling” doctrine. As in Jama v. ICE, we should be especially reluctant to infer omitted requirements where Congress demonstrated elsewhere in the same statutory scheme that it can speak clearly. Bowles v. Russell reinforces that courts must respect statutory time limits and cannot reshape them through equitable doctrines, even when policy arguments (like perverse incentives) have force.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The supervised-release statute provides an express tolling rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (tolling during imprisonment), and that specificity strongly suggests Congress did not authorize additional judge-made tolling for fugitive status—particularly where § 3583(i) supplies a defined mechanism for delayed revocation after expiration when a warrant or summons issues in time. Creating a freestanding “fugitive tolling” doctrine risks extending supervision beyond the term imposed in the judgment, raising rule-of-law and jurisdictional concerns akin to the limits emphasized in Bowles v. Russell. While absconding is serious misconduct, Congress addressed enforcement through revocation and § 3583(i)’s timing requirements rather than an implied tolling regime, and fairness cautions against enlarging custodial exposure by judicial invention. The government can still protect the public by acting promptly (warrant/summons) and seeking revocation for violations that occur within the supervised-release term.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The supervised-release statute specifies when the term "does not run"—most notably in 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) for qualifying imprisonment—and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3583 creates a further, judge-made tolling rule for fugitive status. Under the negative-implication logic this Court applied in United States v. Johnson, 529 U.S. 53 (2000), courts should not add extra tolling exceptions where Congress provided a limited, express one. Section 3583(i) also supplies a workable, text-based mechanism for delayed revocation (issuing a warrant or summons before expiration) without extending the sentence by equitable doctrine. While respondent’s policy concerns are real, Mont v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 1826 (2019), supports reading tolling questions through the statutory text rather than importing free-floating common-law tolling into this distinctly statutory regime.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The supervised-release scheme is statutory, and we should not graft a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule onto it when Congress has addressed timing and jurisdiction expressly elsewhere. Section 3624(e) provides an explicit tolling rule for imprisonment of 30 days or more, and under the negative-implication logic reflected in Jama v. ICE, Congress’s choice to specify that tolling circumstance counsels against implying additional ones for fugitivity. Section 3583(i) likewise supplies a limited mechanism for delayed revocation after a term’s expiration if a warrant or summons issues beforehand, which would be undermined if courts could extend supervision beyond the imposed term through equitable tolling. Consistent with Bowles v. Russell’s insistence that courts not create extra-statutory timing/jurisdictional extensions, the clock continues to run absent clear congressional authorization to stop it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The supervised-release term is a statutory sentence component set by Congress, and absent clear textual authorization courts should be reluctant to create a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that effectively extends the term beyond what the sentencing court imposed under 18 U.S.C. § 3583. Section 3583(i) supplies a specific, workable mechanism for delayed revocation when a warrant or summons issues before expiration, which suggests Congress addressed timing/jurisdiction questions and did not generally authorize tolling for absconding. Consistent with this Court’s insistence that courts not craft equitable exceptions to statutory timing rules, see Bowles v. Russell, petitioner’s supervised-release clock should continue to run unless Congress has expressly provided otherwise. Practical concerns about incentives for flight are serious, but they are better handled through Congress’s chosen tools (including timely warrants and prosecution for new crimes) rather than judicial enlargement of supervision terms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The supervised-release statutes contemplate actual “supervision” during “the term imposed,” 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e), and a supervisee who absconds is not being supervised in any meaningful sense; reading the scheme to award credit for that period would treat noncompliance as service of the sentence. In Mont v. United States, 587 U.S. 514 (2019), the Court held that supervised release does not run during certain periods when the defendant is unavailable for supervision, relying on statutory text sufficient to “stop the clock,” which supports treating fugitivity likewise as time not credited toward completion. Section 3583(i) confirms Congress’s concern with preserving revocation authority when expiration would otherwise defeat enforcement, and it would be anomalous to interpret the framework to allow a defendant to run out the term precisely by evading supervision. While Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), cautions against judge-made exceptions to jurisdictional deadlines, here the better textual reading of the supervised-release scheme—consistent with Mont—denies credit for periods when supervised release cannot be carried out.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3583 establishes a fixed term of supervised release imposed as part of the sentence, and Congress specifically provided a narrow, timing-based mechanism in § 3583(i) to preserve revocation jurisdiction after expiration when a warrant or summons issues before the term ends—suggesting courts should not create a broader, judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that extends supervision beyond its stated length. Mont v. United States interpreted § 3624(e) as expressly tolling supervised release during certain imprisonment, reinforcing that when Congress wants supervised-release time not to run, it knows how to say so, and that courts should be cautious about implying additional tolling categories. Bowles v. Russell underscores that courts should not craft equitable exceptions to statutory timing limits, a concern that applies here where fugitive tolling effectively alters the statutory endpoint of supervision. The government’s practical concerns can be addressed through prompt issuance of warrants/summonses under § 3583(i) and enforcement mechanisms, without expanding supervision through extra-textual doctrines that risk undermining procedural fairness and clear notice.
